title: A 25-Year-Old From Telangana Died on an Indiana Highway. She Is the Latest in a Pattern That No One Wants to Talk About.
excerpt: Navya Gadusu was killed in a two-vehicle crash on Interstate 65 near Crown Point. Her death comes amid a troubling year for Indian students in the United States — and a diaspora that is running out of ways to explain it away.
body:
Navya Gadusu, a 25-year-old Indian student living in Chicago, was pronounced dead at 12:16 a.m. on Saturday, May 17, at Franciscan Health Crown Point in Indiana. The cause of death was blunt force traumatic injuries sustained in a motor vehicle crash on northbound Interstate 65 near mile marker 246.

The Lake County Coroner's office dispatched its medicolegal death investigation team shortly after midnight. Family members later identified the body at the coroner's office. A forensic autopsy was scheduled for Monday, May 18. The Indiana State Police and Tri-Creek EMS are investigating the crash, which also injured six other people.

Gadusu was originally from Cheruvugattu village in Nalgonda district, Telangana. She had moved to Chicago to pursue higher education — one of hundreds of thousands of Indian students who have made the same journey in recent years, drawn by the promise of American universities and the economic opportunities that follow.

The Indian Consulate General in Chicago has expressed condolences and confirmed it is in contact with her family to provide assistance.

A Pattern That Demands Attention

Gadusu's death is not an isolated incident. It comes in a year that has already seen multiple fatalities involving Indian students and Indian-origin individuals in the United States. Earlier in 2026, reports surfaced of an Indian-American student found dead in Ohio, an Indian-origin couple and their daughter killed in a separate car crash, and an Indian student who remains on life support after a stabbing.

The numbers are not tracked systematically — there is no central database of Indian student deaths abroad — but community organisations and consular officials privately acknowledge that the frequency is alarming. The Ministry of External Affairs in Delhi does not publish annual statistics on Indian student fatalities overseas, making it impossible to determine whether the problem is worsening or simply becoming more visible in the age of social media.

What is clear is that road accidents represent a disproportionate share of these tragedies. Unlike campus violence or hate crimes, which attract political attention and institutional response, road deaths are treated as individual misfortunes — routine entries in police blotters, quickly forgotten by everyone except the families left behind.

The Scale of the Student Pipeline

The context matters. India is now the largest source of international students in the United States, having overtaken China in the 2024-25 academic year. According to the Institute of International Education, there are over 340,000 Indian students currently enrolled at American universities, with the number growing at roughly 20 per cent annually.

This pipeline generates enormous economic value — Indian students contribute an estimated $12 billion annually to the US economy through tuition, housing, and living expenses. It also creates a massive population of young Indians navigating American roads, highways, and public transit systems that operate on fundamentally different norms than what they grew up with.

Interstate 65, where Gadusu's crash occurred, is a major north-south corridor connecting Chicago to Indianapolis. The stretch near Crown Point, Indiana, is heavily trafficked and has seen multiple fatal accidents in recent years. For Indian students commuting between Chicago and Indiana — a common pattern for university students visiting friends or attending events — the corridor is familiar but unforgiving.

What Families Back Home Face

For the Gadusu family in Cheruvugattu, the logistics of grief are now layered with the bureaucratic complexity that defines every Indian family's worst nightmare about sending a child abroad. Repatriation of remains, coordination with US law enforcement, dealing with insurance — or the likely absence of adequate coverage — and navigating a legal system in a foreign language, all while processing unspeakable loss.

Consular assistance, while available, is chronically understaffed. The Indian consulate in Chicago covers a vast geographic territory across multiple states, and its ability to provide sustained support to bereaved families is limited by resources. Community organisations — Telugu associations, student groups, GoFundMe campaigns — often fill the gap, but their capacity is equally constrained.

The Conversation the Diaspora Needs to Have

Every few weeks, a name trends briefly in Indian diaspora WhatsApp groups. A young face. A GoFundMe link. A consular condolence statement. And then the conversation moves on, because there is no institutional framework to prevent the next one.

Road safety education for incoming international students is effectively non-existent. Most US universities offer orientation sessions on academic integrity, campus resources, and cultural adjustment — but not on the practical realities of American roads: highway speeds, weather conditions, vehicle maintenance standards, and the differences between Indian and American driving norms.

Some diaspora advocates have called for the Indian government to negotiate bilateral agreements on student safety, similar to frameworks that exist for worker welfare in Gulf countries. Others have pushed for mandatory accident insurance as a condition of student visa issuance. Neither proposal has gained traction.

For now, the pattern continues. Navya Gadusu was 25 years old, from a small village in Telangana, living in Chicago, and driving on a highway in Indiana. She is survived by a family that sent her to America for a better future, and a diaspora that mourns her without knowing how to stop it from happening again.
